claims.text: Increasing local chemical short-range order in multi-element, near-equiatomic nanoparticles will enhance their structural stability at high temperature.
Increasing local chemical short-range order will enhance the nanoparticles' chemical stability at high temperature.
Local chemical order creates a rugged local energy landscape and raises activation barriers.
Local-chemical-order-induced barriers slow atomic diffusion.
Local-chemical-order-induced barriers suppress phase segregation.
Thermal treatment can increase local chemical order.
Dopant additions can be used to increase local chemical order in these nanoparticles.
Use of inert or controlled atmospheres minimizes extrinsic oxidation effects during service testing.
Local chemical order manifests through hard atomic motifs and bond-energy fluctuations.
Local chemical order hinders atomic mobility.
Local chemical order impedes dislocation motion.
Reduced diffusivity impedes thermally activated nanoparticle coarsening.
Reduced diffusivity impedes elemental partitioning.
Local chemical order can preserve a single-phase solid-solution nanoparticle structure at the stated service temperatures.
Nanoparticles with enhanced local chemical order will have lower rates of phase segregation and chemical inhomogeneity than baseline nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles with enhanced local chemical order will retain catalytic or thermoelectric activity better than baseline nanoparticles.
Baseline nanoparticles without tailored local chemical order are expected to undergo measurable phase segregation and chemical instability during long-term high-temperature operation.
Oxidation, impurities, mechanical stresses, or LCO-insensitive diffusion pathways may dominate degradation and obscure the proposed mechanism.
The quantitative local-order threshold required for substantial stability enhancement is not established.
The proposed relationship may not be universal across multi-element compositions and service environments.
